summary:
We built a family-friendly roguelike in Godot about planning and flying a crewed mission to the International Space Station.

Players fill a limited cargo hold with modules drawn from a deck of nearly 60 cards. The cards cover life support (water, oxygen, food, energy), communication, navigation, propulsion and fuel. Each choice changes the rocket's weight, thrust, fuel needs and reliability, and the game shows the resulting launch odds live. After launch, players run a crew through a 10-day mission in real time. They assign astronauts to stations, keep resources balanced, and handle surprise events such as solar storms, equipment failures, and the stress of isolation.

The game turns the trade-offs of real mission design into decisions anyone can make. Every gram has a cost, systems depend on each other, and both the crew's health and their mental wellbeing matter. Nobody ever dies: a failed launch scrubs or splashes down, and struggling astronauts fly home in the return capsule. That makes it safe for kids to experiment, fail, learn about their mistakes and try again. Players learn by playing why spaceflight takes careful planning, redundancy and teamwork.

It is important for middle schoolers to high schoolers who want to fully understand how a mission is handled, from conception to resource management. This is a fun way for them to explore how each amelioration, each choice they make, is going to have a consequence on their survival chance, while learning concrete facts.
details:
Our game is a family-friendly roguelike about a crewed mission to the International Space Station. It has two phases.

1. Plan and launch. Players draft modules into a limited cargo hold from a deck of nearly 60 cards. The cards cover water, oxygen, food, energy, communication, navigation, propulsion and fuel. Every card changes the rocket's weight, thrust, fuel needs and reliability, and a live gauge shows the chance of a good launch. Some cards work better together, and some only when they sit next to each other in the cargo, so packing order matters. If the launch fails, it scrubs on the pad or parachutes into the sea, and the player goes back to planning.

2. Survive the mission. For 10 in-game days, the player runs the crew on a real-time clock from 08:00 to 20:00. They send astronauts to stations to produce resources and fix modules. They also answer about 25 kinds of events, such as solar storms, power failures, isolation and good news. Each event offers several choices, and if nobody answers in time, a default outcome applies. Resources, crew health, and stress are settled each night.

Nobody ever dies. When a crew member reaches their health or stress limit, they fly home safely in the return capsule.

Benefits and intended impact:

The game teaches how real missions are designed by letting players make the decisions themselves:

- every kilogram has a cost

- systems depend on each other

- redundancy matters

- mental health is as important as oxygen

- learning and anticipating the synergies of each card is the key to winning

But failure is gentle and also normal, so children and families can experiment, fail and try again without fear. We want players to come away curious about how missions are really planned, why it failed, with a feel for why spaceflight needs careful trade-offs and teamwork.

Tools and technologies:

- Godot 4.7 game engine, written in GDScript.

- Card system: cards and events are data resources. We used the YARD addon as the card registry.

- Content: designers wrote all card and event text in spreadsheets (CSV), so non-programmers could write content.

- Shaders: custom ones for a CRT screen effect and foil cards.

- Art and audio: pixel art for the ship, crew and cards, plus original music for each phase.

- Balance testing: a headless bot plays the whole game thousands of times. We tuned the numbers until a casual player wins about 60% of the time.

Creativity:

The game combines deck-building with real-time crew management. The mission is narrated through a retro typewriter terminal. Each card comes from one of four fictional nations, and each nation gives a bonus that grows as you carry more of its cards. This nods to the international partnership behind the ISS and rewards cooperation.

Factors we considered:

- Accessibility for all ages, with no death or violence.

- Mechanics grounded in real mission concerns: life support, launch physics, communication and navigation, crew psychology.

- Replay value through random cards and events.

- Difficulty that is challenging but fair, checked by simulation.

- A clear split between the simulation code and the visuals, so a small hackathon team could build quickly.
